description: Havan, puja, japa, bhajan, kirtan and darshan; sacred places; holy people; pilgrimage to Varanasi and the Ganges.
content_html:
Forms of Hindu Worship

Hinduism does not have a single compulsory form of worship. Instead, Hindus practise a rich variety of devotional acts at home, in the temple, outdoors, beside rivers and at sacred sites. These acts are collectively called upasana (drawing close to the divine). The two most widespread forms are havan (also called homa) and puja.

Havan (Homa): The Fire Ceremony

Havan is a sacred fire ritual rooted in the ancient Vedic tradition. A priest (pandit) or family head prepares a fire in a square pit (kund) and feeds it with offerings of clarified butter (ghee), grains, herbs and wood while reciting Sanskrit mantras. The fire is understood to carry the offerings directly to the deities, purifying participants and the surrounding space. Havan is performed at major life-cycle events such as weddings, house-blessings and funerals, as well as at regular temple rituals. In Sanskrit, the word homa comes from a root meaning “to sacrifice or offer.”

Havan reflects the Hindu concept of yajna (sacrifice), one of the three core religious duties alongside dana (giving) and tapas (austerity). The Bhagavad Gita at IX 13–14 describes devoted Hindus who worship God through austerities and yajna. Many Hindus see havan as an act of purification — the fire burns away impurity and the smoke carries prayers upward.

Puja: Devotional Worship

Puja is the central act of Hindu devotional worship, performed both in the home and at the temple (mandir). It involves approaching the murti (sacred image of the deity) and offering a sequence of sixteen services (shodashopachara). These include bathing the murti, dressing it, placing flower garlands around it, burning incense, offering food (prasad), waving a lamp (arati) and prayers. At the end of arati, the flame is passed around worshippers who cup their hands over it and bring the warmth to their faces — receiving the divine blessing.

At home, many Hindu families maintain a small shrine (puja room) where they perform morning and evening devotions. Temple puja is performed by priests on behalf of all worshippers, usually several times a day at appointed hours. The Bhagavad Gita at XII 5 acknowledges that some devotees may find it difficult to meditate on an unmanifest (formless) Brahman, suggesting that murti-based puja offers an accessible route to the divine for those who relate to God in personal form.

Key Fact

Key offerings in puja include water (purification), flowers (beauty), incense (sweet fragrance rising to God), food (prasad — which is then shared with worshippers as divine blessing) and light (arati lamp). Each offering symbolises an aspect of devotion and the giving of the self to God.

Japa, Bhajan and Kirtan

Japa is the practice of repeating a divine name or mantra, silently or quietly, as a form of meditation and devotion. The practitioner often uses a string of prayer beads (mala) to count repetitions — typically 108, a sacred number in Hinduism. Japa is associated with bhakti and raja yoga traditions alike; repeating a mantra such as Om Namah Shivaya or simply “Ram, Ram” is held to calm the mind and draw it towards God. The Gayatri Mantra from the Rig Veda is considered the most sacred of all Hindu mantras; reciting it is believed to bestow wisdom and purify the mind.

Bhajan and kirtan are forms of devotional music central to bhakti practice. Bhajans are lyrical songs addressed to a deity — often Vishnu, Krishna, Rama, Shiva or the Goddess — and may be sung privately or in congregation. Kirtan is specifically call-and-response communal singing in which a lead singer chants and the congregation repeats, often accompanied by harmonium, tabla and cymbals. Kirtan creates an atmosphere of collective devotion and is a prominent feature of temple festivals. The Bhagavad Gita at IX 13–14 describes devoted Hindus who worship the divine through continuous kirtan and firm vows.

Darshan: Beholding the Divine

Darshan means “sight” or “vision.” When a worshipper stands before a murti in the temple, they are not merely looking at a statue — they understand themselves to be in the direct presence of the deity and to be seen by the deity in return. This mutual gaze is the core of the darshan experience: the devotee comes to see God and to receive God’s gaze. The eyes of the murti are therefore the most carefully crafted feature and are formally “opened” in a special ceremony when the image is consecrated.

Darshan also applies to holy people. When devotees visit a living guru or a wandering holy person (sadhu or sadhvi), they seek the guru’s darshan. Simply being in the presence of someone who has advanced on the spiritual path is held to transmit blessings and spiritual merit. This is why pilgrims travel long distances to see famous teachers, even for just a moment.

Hindu worship integrates nature and the divine. The tulsi (holy basil) plant is considered sacred to Vishnu and is placed in puja rooms; watering it is itself an act of worship. The peepal tree is considered a dwelling of Vishnu and is worshipped on certain days. The cow (gau mata, “mother cow”) is revered as a symbol of abundance, non-violence and the earth’s generosity — harming a cow is considered deeply sinful in many Hindu communities. The Ganges (Ganga) is worshipped as a goddess in her own right. This integration of nature and the sacred reflects the Hindu understanding that Brahman pervades all of creation.

Sacred Places and Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage (tirtha yatra) is a central feature of Hindu practice. A tirtha (literally “ford” or “crossing place”) is a sacred site where the boundary between the human and divine worlds is thought to be especially thin. Visiting a tirtha, bathing in sacred waters and receiving darshan at famous temples are believed to generate spiritual merit (punya) and accelerate progress towards moksha. Hinduism has seven especially sacred cities: Varanasi (also called Kashi or Benares) is the most important of these.

Varanasi, on the banks of the river Ganges, is considered the city of Shiva. Dying in Varanasi is believed to guarantee liberation (kashi labh) because Shiva is said to whisper the Taraka mantra (the name of Rama, a liberating sacred name) into the ear of the dying. The burning ghats where bodies are cremated at the river’s edge are perpetually alight. Pilgrims come to bathe in the Ganges at dawn, to attend the spectacular Ganga aarti (fire ceremony at the river), to pray at the Kashi Vishwanath temple and sometimes to bring the ashes of relatives for immersion. Hindus believe that a dip in the Ganges removes accumulated negative karma.

Key Fact

The Kumbh Mela, held at four rotating sacred sites on holy rivers (the Ganges at Prayagraj and Haridwar, the Godavari at Nashik, and the Shipra at Ujjain), is the largest religious gathering on earth, attended by tens of millions of pilgrims. Bathing at the Kumbh Mela during auspicious planetary alignments is believed to wash away all sin and advance the soul towards moksha. It illustrates the centrality of the Ganges in Hindu religious life.

Not all Hindus regard physical pilgrimage as spiritually necessary. The Bhagavad Gita at XII 5 acknowledges the difficulty of worshipping an unmanifest God and offers devotion as a path, but does not insist on specific sacred sites. Some traditions within Advaita Vedanta hold that Brahman is equally present everywhere and that a purified inner state matters more than external location. The medieval poet-saint Tukaram taught that God is found in the heart, not only at Varanasi. This divergence between those who value sacred sites and those who prioritise inner realization is a genuine debate within Hinduism and is worth exploring in the 15-mark Discuss question.
exam_tip_html: In Outline and Explain questions about Hindu worship, be precise with terminology: puja is specifically the ritual worship of a murti with offerings; havan is the fire ceremony; darshan is beholding the divine. Examiners distinguish candidates who use specific terms from those who give vague answers about ‘praying.’ For the 15-mark Discuss, if asked whether pilgrimage is necessary for salvation, name Varanasi and the Ganges and include a divergent view — for example, that Advaita Vedanta and teachers like Tukaram locate liberation in inner realisation, not external place. Spell darshan, prasad, murti and Varanasi accurately, as SPaG is assessed on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hindu worship takes many forms: havan (fire ceremony), puja (devotional offering to a murti), japa (mantra repetition), bhajan and kirtan (devotional music). All aim to draw the worshipper closer to the divine.
  • Darshan — the auspicious sight of a deity’s image or a holy person — is at the heart of Hindu temple worship. Being seen by the deity is as important as seeing the deity.
  • Pilgrimage to sacred sites, especially Varanasi on the river Ganges, is valued as a source of spiritual merit and a path towards moksha, though some Hindu thinkers argue that inner realisation matters more than outward travel.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'puja' in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks:
Any accurate one-sentence description for 1 mark. For example:
• Puja is a form of devotional worship offered to a deity image (murti), involving offerings such as flowers, incense, food and light.
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Hindus do during a havan ceremony.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A havan is a fire ceremony in which offerings such as ghee, grains and wood are made into a sacred fire.
• Sanskrit mantras are recited by a priest or family member as offerings are made.
• The fire is understood to carry offerings to the deities and to purify the participants.
• Havan is performed at life-cycle events such as weddings and at regular temple rituals.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes the purpose or context of havan.]

practice_questions.text: Outline the importance of darshan for Hindu worshippers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Darshan means ‘sight’ or ‘vision.’ When a worshipper stands before a murti, they understand themselves to be in the presence of the deity and to be seen by the deity.
• This mutual gaze is experienced as a blessing: the devotee comes to see God and to receive God’s gaze.
• Darshan also applies to holy people (gurus, sadhus): being in the presence of a spiritually advanced person is held to transmit blessings.
• Pilgrims travel great distances for the darshan of famous gurus or at celebrated temples.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a clear, developed outline that includes more than one form of darshan or explains the spiritual significance.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Varanasi is an important pilgrimage destination for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Varanasi is situated on the banks of the sacred river Ganges, which is worshipped as the goddess Ganga. Bathing in the Ganges is believed to cleanse accumulated negative karma and to bring the soul closer to moksha. This makes the city the most spiritually powerful bathing place in Hinduism.
• Varanasi is considered the city of Shiva. Dying in Varanasi is believed to guarantee liberation (kashi labh) because Shiva is said to whisper the liberating mantra into the ear of the dying. Hindus therefore bring seriously ill relatives there to die, and the burning ghats are permanently alight with cremation fires.
• The Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas — the most sacred shrines to Shiva. Receiving darshan there is a major source of spiritual merit.
• The Ganga aarti (fire ceremony at the river at dawn and dusk) is a powerful collective act of worship that draws thousands of pilgrims daily.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per reason — 1 for identifying the reason, 2 for development, 3 for development with a specific Hindu belief or concept such as karma, moksha or darshan.]

practice_questions.text: 'Pilgrimage to a sacred place is the most important Hindu practice.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Pilgrimage to Varanasi and the river Ganges is among the most deeply embedded practices in popular Hinduism. Millions undertake pilgrimages each year, suggesting it holds central significance for many believers.
• The belief that dying in Varanasi guarantees moksha makes pilgrimage uniquely powerful: no other practice is believed to guarantee liberation with such certainty.
• The Kumbh Mela, the largest religious gathering on earth, demonstrates the enormous practical and emotional importance Hindus place on bathing at sacred sites during auspicious planetary alignments.
• Receiving darshan at a famous murti or sacred site is held to generate spiritual merit (punya) that accelerates progress toward moksha.

Arguments against:
• The Bhagavad Gita presents four margas — jnana, bhakti, karma and raja yoga — none of which requires pilgrimage to a specific place. A householder practising selfless service (sewa) may progress just as effectively.
• Many Hindu thinkers, including those in the Advaita Vedanta tradition, hold that Brahman is present everywhere equally. The medieval saint Tukaram and others taught that liberation is found in the purified heart, not at a sacred site.
• Home puja performed daily can be argued to be more important because it is sustained, everyday devotion rather than a once-in-a-lifetime journey. The Bhagavad Gita at XII 5 suggests that devotion in any form is accepted by God.
• Karma yoga, the path of selfless social action (sewa, dana), can be argued to be more important in the modern world: it transforms society rather than simply securing individual spiritual merit.

Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources and concepts (Bhagavad Gita XII 5; karma, moksha, punya; Varanasi; Tukaram); explicit weighing of arguments; a reasoned conclusion that justifies a position.
Secure: Two clear sides with some development; at least one named source or sacred site; a conclusion.
Developing: One side more developed; limited use of sources; partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of a guru in Hindu worship and pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A guru is a spiritual teacher who guides disciples on the path to liberation through personal example and instruction.
• Receiving the darshan of a guru is considered a source of blessing and spiritual merit.
• Pilgrims often travel to a guru’s ashram (hermitage) as a form of pilgrimage, seeking guidance and transmission of spiritual energy.
• Sadhus (wandering ascetics) also provide darshan; their presence at sacred sites such as Varanasi enhances those sites’ spiritual power.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes at least two aspects of the guru’s role.]

glossary_terms.definition: A Hindu fire ceremony in which offerings such as ghee, grain and wood are made into a sacred fire with Sanskrit mantras as an act of purification and worship.
Ritual devotional worship of a deity image (murti), involving offerings of water, flowers, incense, food and light.
A sacred image or statue of a deity used as the focus of Hindu worship; considered by devotees to be an actual presence of the divine.
The meditative repetition of a divine name, mantra or short prayer, often counted on a mala (prayer beads).
Devotional songs addressed to a deity, performed individually or in congregation as an act of bhakti worship.
Communal call-and-response devotional singing, often accompanied by instruments; a central feature of bhakti worship.
The auspicious sight of a deity's image or a holy person; being seen by the divine is itself considered a spiritual blessing.
An ancient mantra from the Rig Veda, considered the most sacred in Hinduism; reciting it is believed to bestow wisdom and purity.
A spiritual teacher in Hinduism who guides disciples on the path to liberation through personal example and instruction.
A Hindu ascetic who has renounced worldly life to seek spiritual liberation; sadhvis are the female equivalent.
The holiest city in Hinduism, on the banks of the Ganges; considered Shiva's city, where dying is believed to guarantee liberation.
A journey to a sacred place (tirtha) undertaken for spiritual merit; visiting such sites is believed to advance the soul towards moksha.
